title: MCP across Everpure, Nutanix, and Kubernetes
summary: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers let an AI assistant query Everpure, Nutanix, and Kubernetes data for capacity, incident, and recovery insights
body_markdown:
### Summary


With Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, an AI assistant can access Everpure, Nutanix, and Kubernetes data to provide insight into capacity, incident timelines, and workload recoverability.


*Part 1 of a series*


Infrastructure tooling overlaps a lot more than it used to. For example, when connected to Everpure™[FlashArray](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/block-file-object-storage.html) ™,[Nutanix Prism Central knows quite a bit of important information](https://blog.everpuredata.com/products/more-than-block-storage-3-ways-everpure-connects-your-nutanix-infrastructure/) about the FlashArray system backing its storage container(s). Other monitoring tools can span multiple layers as well, which means a lot of day-to-day questions can now be answered from a single console.


The trouble is that the coverage is uneven, and the boundaries are not always where you would expect. One system’s view of storage stops somewhere that isn’t where the next system’s view begins, and the gap between them usually isn’t obvious. Often, you find it by chance.


That’s fine until you need to ask a question that spans that gap, and a lot of the important questions do. What applications could fail if this FlashArray system goes offline? What changed in the hour before last night’s incident? Is that mission-critical VM as protected as I think it is?


Every one of those questions has an answer. The obstacle isn’t that the data is missing; it’s that the data is scattered across different systems, and each system gives you a different view of what’s happening. Answering a question that blends those boundaries has traditionally meant pulling information from several places, matching things up, and knowing enough about each system to make sense of the result.


That limits what people ask. You deal with the alert, close the ticket, and move on. You don’t always get to the next question, even though that’s often where the more interesting and informative answers are.


## **Getting separate systems into the same conversation**


This led to a question: How do you bring all of these different systems into the same conversation without building a deep custom integration between every pair?


For this experiment, the answer was Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP gives the AI assistant, in our case Claude Desktop, a standard way to interact with different products, so each platform can expose the information it already has without requiring deeper integration with the other platforms. In our case, that meant giving the assistant separate MCP access to the storage, virtualization, and Kubernetes layers and seeing what it could do with them together.


Two MCP servers came from Everpure. The[Everpure Fusion™ MCP server](https://github.com/PureStorage-OpenConnect/fusion-mcp-server) provides access to one or more FlashArray systems (or[FlashBlade](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/unstructured-data-storage.html) ® systems) using API credentials you configure, giving the assistant information about[volumes, capacity, data reduction, and performance](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/smarter-ai-powered-data-management-with-everpure-fusion-mcp-server-2/) across those arrays.[Pure1® Manage MCP server](https://purecommunity.purestorage.com/blog/user-blogs/enabling-agentic-ai-via-pure1-manage-mcp-server/3771) gives us information about the[broader Pure1 environment](https://blog.everpuredata.com/products/pure1-now-agentic/) : fleet inventory, hardware, alerts, support contracts, and—less obviously—subscriptions and invoices.


The third MCP server is[Nutanix’s server for Prism Central](https://github.com/nutanix/ntnx-api-mcp-server) , which gives us virtual machines, clusters, hosts, storage containers, tasks, and alerts. It also provides utilization and performance information about the Nutanix environment itself, such as how much CPU and memory a VM is consuming or how heavily an AHV host or cluster is being utilized.


The fourth is a[Kubernetes MCP server](https://github.com/containers/kubernetes-mcp-server) , pointed in our case at Nutanix Kubernetes Platform with[Portworx® CSI (PX-CSI)](https://docs.portworx.com/portworx-csi/) underneath. That gives us nodes, pods, persistent volume claims, storage classes, and events. Together, these give the assistant visibility into several different layers of the environment.


Setting all of this up is surprisingly straightforward. The three on-premises servers take a download and a few lines of client configuration on your laptop, while Pure1 Manage uses a minted token. For example, Everpure Fusion can be authenticated once against the FlashArray system, then added to Claude Desktop through its MCP configuration file.


```text
fusion-mcp-server generate-config --FA fa1.example.com,<api-token>
```


The following is an example of the Claude Desktop MCP configuration that starts both servers. On Windows, this file is located at *%APPDATA%\\Claude\\claude_desktop_config.json.* On macOS, it’s located at *~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json.*


```text
{
"mcpServers": {
"fusion-mcp": {
"command": "C:/Tools/fusion-mcp-server.exe",
"args": [
"start",
"--auth-config",
"C:/Users/you/.config/fusion-mcp/auth-config.json"
]
},
"nutanix": {
"command": "C:/nutanix/.venv/Scripts/nutanix-mcp.exe",
"args": ["serve-stdio"],
"env": {
"PC_HOST": "10.21.10.10",
"PC_USERNAME": "your-pc-user",
"PC_PASSWORD": "your-pc-password",
"READ_ONLY_MODE": "true"
}
}
}
}
```


## **What the assistant adds**


Obviously, the MCP servers don’t talk to each other. Each MCP server has a view into exactly one solution and knows nothing about the others. There is no shared schema and no middleware coordinating these disparate products behind the scenes. Nor should there be.


The interesting part is what happens when you put those systems in front of an AI assistant and let it work across and correlate the information they provide.


The assistant isn’t just relaying calls. It can pull information from the different systems, understand enough about the context to put those answers together, and give you a single answer to a question that would otherwise require several separate investigations.


It also changes what asking questions feels like. You don’t compose a query, run it, read a report, and then go back and figure out how to update the query to get the information you actually want. You ask something, look at what comes back, and follow up from there: *now break that down by cluster; ignore anything under a terabyte; which of those have snapshots?* Each turn reshapes the next set of calls. Each question builds on the last, so the analysis happens naturally as part of the conversation.


That can matter more than any individual answer. The third and fourth questions are usually the good ones, and nobody ever got to them before because the work and time required to answer them was too high.


The useful part is that the systems already contain the connections you need. A Nutanix virtual disk can point you toward the storage volume backing it, along with information about whether that volume is protected through Prism or a FlashArray protection policy. Prism knows about the[external storage registered with it](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/new-features-expand-everpure-and-nutanix-joint-solution/) , and the FlashArray system knows about the volumes it owns. Those relationships have always existed. The difference is that you can now ask about them directly without manually walking through each system.


## **Some useful examples**


One example is capacity reporting. A FlashArray Pod quota is based on provisioned capacity, not the amount of physical space actually being consumed. That means Prism can reach the Pod quota and stop creating new volumes even while the FlashArray system still shows plenty of free capacity. Everpure[documents this](https://support.everpuredata.com/r/nutanix/understanding-flasharray-pod-quotas-and-capacity-reporting-with-nutanix) and recommends against setting a Pod quota for this reason. For argument’s sake, though, it makes a useful example because the problem only becomes clear when you look at both systems together.


Looking at either system by itself can make the environment appear healthy. Looking at both together gives you the full picture: what capacity Prism has provisioned, what quota is configured and where, and how much space on the FlashArray system is actually consumed.


The screenshot below shows an actual result from Claude Desktop as another example. We asked it to summarize several capacity and utilization metrics across our Nutanix and FlashArray environments. To answer the questions, Claude used multiple MCP servers, chose the appropriate source for each metric, and combined data from both systems where needed.


*Figure 1: Claude Desktop using Nutanix and Everpure Fusion MCP servers to build a combined view of capacity, utilization, and data reduction.*


Incident timelines can be assembled from multiple sources at once. FlashArray audit logs, fleet events, AHV hypervisor tasks, and cluster events all describe the same 10 minutes in four different formats. Merging them by hand is tedious enough that people mostly don’t do it unless it’s especially critical, which means the context that could explain an incident is often sitting in separate consoles rather than in one timeline.


Recoverability becomes one answer instead of three partial ones. Which volumes have snapshots? Which machines have recovery points? Which workloads are replicated, and what does that mean for expected vs. actual RPO?


## **Two important notes**


Start with your MCP servers in read-only mode.[The Nutanix MCP server](https://github.com/nutanix/ntnx-api-mcp-server) is also in technical preview as of this writing and should not be used against production clusters. Everything shown in this post is for inspection only, which is a good place to start because the value is high and the risk is low. Some MCP servers can also be configured to make changes in the environment, so understand the impact before enabling that kind of access.


The other caveat is that the assistant is doing the reasoning, which means it can reason incorrectly. Ask it to show its sources for every number. If it can’t name where a figure came from, don’t put it in a slide or in a Slack message. The nice thing about this approach is that the provenance can be part of the answer; use it.


## **Up next**


There are more interesting questions to explore once all of this is connected.


Where should a new demanding workload run based on both Nutanix and FlashArray utilization? What changes, what risks, and what advantages occur when we move beyond read-only and let the assistant take action? And where do we have capacity that isn’t being used?


That’s the next step: moving from simply finding information to using information across the environment to make decisions and, eventually, act on them.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


1. **How do you connect an AI assistant to storage, virtualization and Kubernetes at once?** Give it one MCP server per layer (Everpure Fusion, Pure1 Manage, Nutanix Prism Central, a Kubernetes MCP server) in the client config. The servers do not talk to each other; the assistant correlates their answers.
2. **Is it safe to use MCP servers on production infrastructure?** Start in read-only mode. The Nutanix MCP server is in technical preview and should not be used against production clusters. Ask the assistant to name the source of every number.
3. **Why can Prism Central hit a Pod quota while the FlashArray shows free space?** The Pod quota is based on provisioned capacity, not physical consumption, which is why Everpure recommends against setting one.
4. **What can an AI assistant answer across Nutanix and FlashArray that one console cannot?** Capacity against quota, a merged incident timeline across arrays, fleet events and hypervisor tasks, and which volumes and VMs have snapshots, recovery points or replication.
